content:
Doris "Dorie" Miller (October 12, 1919 – November 24, 1943) was a United States Navy cook who became a hero during the attack on Pearl Harbor for his bravery and quick thinking. Despite racial discrimination and segregation in the military at the time, Miller's actions earned him national recognition and made him a symbol of courage and resilience.

### **Early Life**
- **Born:** October 12, 1919, in Waco, Texas.
- **Family:** The third of four sons in a family of sharecroppers. His parents, Conor and Henrietta Miller, worked on a farm.
- **Education:** Attended Waco’s A.J. Moore High School, where he played football as a fullback. He left school to work on his family’s farm and later as a bellhop.
- **Enlistment:** Joined the U.S. Navy in September 1939 as a **Mess Attendant, Third Class**—one of the few positions open to Black sailors at the time due to racial segregation.

### **Military Service & Pearl Harbor (December 7, 1941)**
- **Assignment:** Served aboard the **USS West Virginia (BB-48)**, a battleship stationed at Pearl Harbor.
- **Role:** As a mess attendant, Miller was not trained in combat or gunnery (Black sailors were typically restricted to service roles).
- **Attack on Pearl Harbor:**
  - When the Japanese attack began at around 8:00 AM, Miller was below deck collecting laundry.
  - He rushed to his battle station (the ship’s magazine) but was ordered to help move wounded sailors, including the ship’s captain, **Mervyn Bennion**, who was mortally wounded.
  - Miller then manned a **.50-caliber Browning anti-aircraft machine gun**—a weapon he had no formal training on—and fired at Japanese planes until he ran out of ammunition.
  - He was credited with **downing at least one enemy plane** (though some accounts suggest more).
  - After the gun jammed, he helped carry the dying Captain Bennion to safety before the ship was abandon due to flooding.
  - The **USS West Virginia** sank, but Miller survived.

### **Aftermath & Recognition**
- **Initial Lack of Recognition:** Due to racial biases, Miller’s actions were initially overlooked in early reports.
- **Medal of Honor (Navy Cross):** On **May 27, 1942**, he became the **first Black American to receive the Navy Cross** (the Navy’s second-highest honor at the time) for his actions.
  - **Citation:** *"For distinguished devotion to duty, extraordinary courage and disregard for his own safety during the attack... manning a machine gun and displaying outstanding bravery and coolness under fire."*
  - **Awarded by:** Admiral **Chester W. Nimitz**, commander of the Pacific Fleet.
- **Promotion:** Advanced to **Mess Attendant, First Class** (the highest rank then available to Black sailors in that role).
- **Public Acclaim:**
  - His story was widely publicized in Black newspapers like the **Pittsburgh Courier**, which campaigned for his recognition.
  - The **NAACP** used his example to push for greater racial integration in the military.
  - He became a **warbond salesman** and gave speeches across the U.S. to support the war effort.

### **Later Service & Death**
- **USS Liscome Bay (CVE-56):**
  - After Pearl Harbor, Miller was assigned to the **escort carrier USS Liscome Bay** as a **Mess Attendant, First Class**.
  - On **November 24, 1943**, during the **Battle of Makin (Gilbert Islands)**, a Japanese torpedo struck the ship, causing a magazine explosion.
  - The **Liscome Bay sank in 23 minutes**, and **Miller was among the 646 men killed** (only 272 survived).
  - His body was never recovered.

### **Legacy & Honors**
- **USS Miller (FF-1091):** A **Knox-class frigate** (1973–1991) was named in his honor—the **first U.S. Navy ship named after an African American sailor**.
- **Dorie Miller Memorials:**
  - **Waco, Texas:** A **statue** and **historical marker** honor him.
  - **Pearl Harbor:** A **plaque** at the **USS Arizona Memorial** commemorates his bravery.
  - **Navy Buildings:** The **Dorie Miller Recreation Center** (Great Lakes Naval Station) and a **galley** at the U.S. Naval Academy bear his name.
- **Posthumous Promotions:**
  - In **2010**, the Navy **posthumously promoted Miller to Chief Petty Officer (Mess Management Specialist)**.
  - In **2020**, the Navy **redecorated his Navy Cross to the Medal of Honor** (though this was later **reversed** in 2022 due to procedural issues).
- **Cultural Impact:**
  - **Movies & Books:** Featured in documentaries like *The War* (2007) by Ken Burns and books on Black military history.
  - **Inspiration:** His story inspired generations of Black service members and civil rights activists.

### **Controversies & Unresolved Questions**
- **Medal of Honor Denial:** Despite petitions (including from **Rep. Eddie Bernice Johnson_), the **Medal of Honor** was never officially awarded to him, though some argue he deserved it.
- **Racial Discrimination:** Miller’s case highlights the **segregation and limited opportunities** for Black sailors in WWII. Many believe his race delayed his initial recognition.
- **Exact Actions at Pearl Harbor:** Some accounts suggest he may have shot down **multiple planes**, but official records confirm at least one.

### **Why Dorie Miller Matters**
Doris Miller’s story is a **landmark in military and civil rights history**. He proved that **courage and skill were not bounded by race**, helping pave the way for the **desegregation of the U.S. military** (officially ordered by **President Truman in 1948**).
